claims.claim: The protective effect of CAR-1 K185R against Aβ toxicity is DAF-16-dependent.
claims.source: The protective effect of CAR-1 K185R is DAF-16-dependent, since no protection was seen when EHC124 worms were treated with daf-16 RNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by paralysis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: car-1 RNAi decreases the number of body bends in polyQ67-YFP worms at day 4 of adulthood.
claims.source: In contrast, car-1 RNAi treatment decreased the number of body bends at day 4 of adulthood (p<0.001) but not at day 1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: car-1 RNAi enhances paralysis of polyQ35-YFP worms but not of polyQ35-YFP/glp-1 animals.
claims.source: While daf-2 RNAi protected worms of both strains from paralysis, car-1 RNAi enhanced paralysis of polyQ35-YFP worms but not of polyQ35-YFP/glp-1 animals (A).
claims.evidence: Supported by paralysis assay data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: The knockdown of cgh-1 significantly increases the rates of paralysis in Aβ worms.
claims.source: We let Aβ worms develop on EV bacteria or treated them with RNAi towards daf-2, car-1, or cgh-1, followed their rates of paralysis and found that the knockdown of cgh-1 as well as of car-1, significantly (p<0.035) increase the rates of paralysis compared to untreated worms (Figure 5, C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by paralysis assay data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: car-1 RNAi has no significant effect on heat stress resistance in CF512 and N2 worms.
claims.source: We observed no significant effect of car-1 RNAi on resistance to heat (Figure 6, A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by heat stress survival data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: The expression of CAR-1 K185R elevates survival after heat shock compared to control worms.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the expression of CAR-1 K185R elevated the survival after heat shock compared to control worms (N2, p<0.04), however a trend but not a significant effect was observed when the natural car-1 was over-expressed (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by heat stress survival data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: car-1 RNAi has a small but significant protective effect against pathogenic bacteria P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: Interestingly, car-1 RNAi had a small but significant protective effect from pathogenic bacteria (mean survival of 6.77 ± 0.21 days, p<0.001, Figure 6E, Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by survival data on P. aeruginosa shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: car-1 RNAi increases survival rate of worms exposed to sub-lethal UV radiation.
claims.source: The knockdown of daf-2 protected the worms from UV and the survival rate of the worms treated with car-1 RNAi was also increased compared to control animals (mean survival rates of 10.45 ± 0.22 (daf-2 RNAi), 9.23 ± 0.22 (car-1 RNAi) and 7.97 ± 0.21 (EV) days, respectively, p<0.001) (Figure 6G, Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by UV radiation survival data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The over-expression of wild-type CAR-1 or CAR-1 K185R shortens survival of worms exposed to UV radiation.
claims.source: Similarly, the over-expression of the wild-type CAR-1 or of the CAR-1 K185R mutant significantly shortened the lifespans of worms that were exposed to UV radiation (mean survivals of 12.78 ± 0.33 (EV), 8.89 ± 0.19 (wt CAR-1) and 10.87 ± 0.27 (CAR-1 K185R) days, p<0.001) (Figure 6H and Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by UV radiation survival data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: CAR-1 is an RNA-binding protein that acts in association with the RNA helicase CGH-1 in the germline.
claims.source: CAR-1 is an RNA-binding protein, which acts in association with the RNA helicase, CGH-1 in the germline (Audhya et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Audhya et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 increases the levels of GLP-1 during late oogenesis.
claims.source: The knockdown of car-1 increases the levels of GLP-1 during late oogenesis (Noble et al., 2008), thereby leading to germ cell death and to defective embryonic cytokinesis (Boag et al., 2005; Squirrell et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Noble et al., 2008; Boag et al., 2005; Squirrell et al., 2006.

claims.claim: IIS reduction extends lifespan and elevates stress resistance of worms, mice, and presumably humans.
claims.source: Among these, most prominent is IIS reduction, which extends lifespan and elevates stress resistance of worms (Kenyon et al., 1993), mice (Holzenberger et al., 2003), and presumably humans (Suh et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies in worms (Kenyon et al., 1993), mice (Holzenberger et al., 2003), and humans (Suh et al., 2008).

claims.claim: DAF-2 initiates a signaling cascade that negatively regulates the activity of at least three transcription factors by modulating phosphorylation.
claims.source: In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans), the sole insulin/IGF receptor, DAF-2, initiates a signaling cascade that negatively regulates the activity of at least three transcription factors by modulating phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: Supported by established knowledge of IIS pathway in C. elegans.

claims.claim: Direct phosphorylation of DAF-16/FOXO prevents this factor from entering the nucleus and regulating target genes.
claims.source: Direct phosphorylation of DAF-16/FOXO (Lee et al., 2001) and of SKN-1/NRF (Tullet et al., 2008) prevents these factors from entering the nucleus and from regulating their target genes.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2001.

claims.claim: IIS reduction protects worms and mice from toxic aggregation of various neurodegeneration-causing proteins.
claims.source: In addition, IIS reduction protects worms and mice from toxic aggregation (proteotoxicity) of various neurodegeneration-causing proteins (reviewed in Carvalhal Marques et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to review by Carvalhal Marques et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Knocking down daf-2 by RNAi reduces the worm's brood size but extends the reproduction period.
claims.source: Finally, IIS reduction also modulates reproduction and egg-laying patterns, as knocking down daf-2 by RNAi, reduces the worm's brood size but extends the reproduction period (Dillin et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dillin et al., 2002.

claims.claim: The ablation of germ cells extends lifespan in C. elegans.
claims.source: Moreover, despite the evidences that the ablation of germ cells extends lifespan (Hsin and Kenyon, 1999) and promotes proteostasis in C. elegans (Shemesh et al., 2013), it is unclear how the aging-regulating mechanisms downstream of the IIS and those that are activated by the reproduction system are linked, and whether post-translational modifications play roles in the orchestration of these mechanisms.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hsin and Kenyon, 1999 and Shemesh et al., 2013.

claims.claim: SUMOylation is a post-translational modification involving reversible covalent attachment of SUMO to specific lysine residues of proteins.
claims.source: SUMOylation is a post-translational modification involving a reversible covalent attachment of a small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) to specific lysine residues of proteins (Melchior, 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Melchior, 2000 and established knowledge of SUMOylation.

claims.claim: C. elegans expresses only one SUMO-encoding gene, smo-1.
claims.source: While mammals ubiquitously express three forms of SUMO (SUMO-1, 2, and 3), C. elegans expresses only one SUMO-encoding gene, smo-1 that encodes a polypeptide of 91 amino acids with a predicted molecular weight of 10.2 kDa (Choudhury and Li, 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Choudhury and Li, 1997.

claims.claim: smo-1 is critically needed for germline development and fertility of C. elegans.
claims.source: Among other functions, smo-1 is critically needed for germline development and fertility of the nematode (Broday, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Broday, 2017.

claims.claim: CAR-1 mediates its aging-altering functions at least partially through the notch-like receptor glp-1.
claims.source: A mechanistic analysis indicated that CAR-1 mediates its aging-altering functions, at least partially, through the notch-like receptor glp-1.
claims.evidence: Supported by experiments showing that car-1 RNAi does not affect lifespan in glp-1 or kri-1 mutant worms.

claims.claim: CAR-1 negatively regulates GLP-1 activity.
claims.source: One possible explanation to the lifespan shortening effect of car-1 RNAi, and the longevity conferred by CAR-1 K185R, suggests that CAR-1 modulates lifespan by negatively regulating the activity of GLP-1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that car-1 RNAi does not shorten lifespan in glp-1 mutant worms and that car-1 RNAi increases sygl-1 expression.

claims.claim: SUMOylation of CAR-1 on lysine 185 plays a role in lifespan determination.
claims.source: In contrast, no lifespan extension was observed in worms that overexpress CAR-1 K257R (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 3) or wild-type CAR-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C and Supplementary file 3), indicating that the SUMOylation of CAR-1 on lysine 185, but not on lysine 257, plays a role in lifespan determination.
claims.evidence: Supported by differential lifespan effects of CAR-1 K185R versus CAR-1 K257R mutations.

claims.claim: CAR-1 regulates lifespan by both DAF-16-dependent and DAF-16-independent mechanisms.
claims.source: These results suggest that CAR-1 also regulates lifespan by a DAF-16-independent mechanism.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that daf-16 RNAi in CAR-1 K185R worms reduces lifespan to wild-type levels but not below, unlike typical daf-16 mutants.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 has no effect on the number of germ cells in wild-type worms.
claims.source: We found that the knockdown of car-1 by RNAi had no significant effect on the number of germ cells as untreated and car-1 RNAi-treated animals had similar numbers of germ cells (Figure 3, C and D; average of 724 ± 45.25 and 719 ± 32.36 cells, respectively).
claims.evidence: Supported by germ cell counting data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: Worms that over-express natural CAR-1 have significantly fewer germ cells compared to untreated worms.
claims.source: In contrast, worms that over-express the natural CAR-1 (EHC117) had significantly less germ cells compared to untreated or car-1 RNAi-treated worms (414.2 ± 6.3 cells, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: Supported by germ cell counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 renders daf-2 and daf-16 mutant worms nearly sterile.
claims.source: Surprisingly, RNAi-mediated knockdown of car-1 resulted in nearly complete sterility of both daf-2 and daf-16 mutant worms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by egg-laying assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 affects neither egg-laying patterns nor brood sizes of daf-9 and daf-12 mutant worms.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, the knockdown of car-1 affects neither egg-laying patterns, nor brood size of daf-9 and daf-12 mutant worms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by egg-laying assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and 2F.

claims.claim: GLP-1 positively regulates the expression of sygl-1 and lst-1.
claims.source: While an increase in the expression levels of both genes was observed in N2 worms upon exposure to 25°C (a significant increase for sygl-1 and a non-significant trend for lst-1), the inactivation of GLP-1 in CF1903 worms, by exposing them to 25°C during development, resulted in a significant reduction in the expression of both, sygl-1 and lst-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, A and B). These results indicate that GLP-1 positively regulates the expression of these two genes.
claims.evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: CAR-1 negatively controls the activity of GLP-1 as a transcriptional regulator of sygl-1.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed significantly elevated levels of sygl-1 in e1370 animals (Figure 3I). A non-significant elevation in the expression of sygl-1 was also seen in car-1 RNAi-treated N2 worms (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). This lack of significance may be explained by the low activity of CAR-1 in these worms, due to its SUMOylation. These results indicate that CAR-1 negatively controls the activity of GLP-1 as a transcriptional regulator of sygl-1.
claims.evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing increased sygl-1 expression upon car-1 knockdown.

claims.claim: CAR-1 plays opposing roles on the expression levels of different GLP-1 target genes.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, the knockdown of car-1 reduced the expression level of lst-1 in e1370 worms (Figure 3I) showing that CAR-1 could play opposing roles on the expression levels of GLP-1 target genes.
claims.evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing decreased lst-1 expression upon car-1 knockdown.

claims.claim: CAR-1 controls proteostasis through GLP-1.
claims.source: This set of experiments shows that knocking down car-1 has no deleterious effect on proteostasis when glp-1 is inactive (p<0.05), indicating that CAR-1 controls proteostasis through GLP-1.
claims.evidence: Supported by paralysis assay data showing that car-1 RNAi does not enhance paralysis in glp-1 mutant worms expressing polyQ35-YFP.

claims.claim: CGH-1 modulates lifespan.
claims.source: Since the CAR-1-associated helicase CGH-1, which is expressed in meiotic germ cells, modulates lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5 and (Seo et al., 2015)), we tested whether this helicase also controls proteostasis.
claims.evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citation to Seo et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The knockdown of cgh-1 significantly increases the rates of paralysis in Aβ worms.
claims.source: To address this, we let Aβ worms develop on EV bacteria or treated them with RNAi towards daf-2, car-1, or cgh-1, followed their rates of paralysis and found that the knockdown of cgh-1 as well as of car-1, significantly (p<0.035) increase the rates of paralysis compared to untreated worms (Figure 5, C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by paralysis assay data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: CAR-1 and CGH-1 promote proteostasis by modulating germ cell activity, plausibly by negatively regulating GLP-1.
claims.source: These results further support the view that CAR-1 and CGH-1 promote proteostasis by modulating germ cell activity, plausibly by negatively regulating GLP-1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that both car-1 and cgh-1 RNAi enhance proteotoxicity and that car-1 RNAi does not affect proteostasis in glp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: The ability to resist stresses such as heat and oxidation are not necessarily coupled with lifespan determination.
claims.source: These results support the theme that the ability to resist stresses such as heat (Maman et al., 2013; Volovik et al., 2014b) and oxidation (Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2012) are not necessarily coupled with lifespan determination.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Maman et al., 2013; Volovik et al., 2014b; Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2012.

claims.claim: IIS reduction by daf-2 RNAi or mutation hyperactivates downstream transcription factors, creating long-lived worms.
claims.source: Thus, IIS reduction by daf-2 RNA interference (RNAi) or by mutation, hyperactivates its downstream transcription factors, creating long-lived worms (Kenyon, 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kenyon, 2005 and established knowledge of IIS pathway.

claims.claim: IIS reduction elevates resistance to heat, UV radiation, and pathogenic bacteria.
claims.source: IIS reduction also elevates resistance to a variety of stresses including heat (Lithgow et al., 1995), ultraviolet (UV) radiation (Murakami and Johnson, 1996), and pathogenic bacteria (Singh and Aballay, 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Lithgow et al., 1995; Murakami and Johnson, 1996; Singh and Aballay, 2006.

claims.claim: Knocking down daf-2 extends lifespan solely during reproductive adulthood.
claims.source: First, knocking down daf-2 extends lifespan solely during reproductive adulthood (Dillin et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dillin et al., 2002.

claims.claim: DAF-16 is essential for the longevity phenotype resulting from both IIS reduction and loss of germ cells.
claims.source: Moreover, the key roles of DAF-16 in the longevity phenotype that results from both, IIS reduction (Kenyon et al., 1993) and loss of germ cells (Berman and Kenyon, 2006), further support the idea that the IIS and germline are inter-related.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kenyon et al., 1993 and Berman and Kenyon, 2006.

claims.claim: DAF-2 signaling governs oogenesis through the RAS-ERK pathway according to food availability.
claims.source: Indeed, DAF-2 signaling was reported to govern oogenesis through the RAS-ERK pathway according to food availability (Lopez et al., 2013) and the phosphatase DAF-18/PTEN locally antagonizes IIS activity in the germline (Narbonne et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Lopez et al., 2013 and Narbonne et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Germline signaling synergizes the longevity mechanisms downstream of the IIS and TOR pathways.
claims.source: In addition, germline signaling synergizes the longevity mechanisms downstream of the IIS and of the target of rapamycin (TOR) pathway (Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: By SUMOylating CAR-1, the IIS suppresses its activity, thereby activating glp-1 to shorten lifespan and impair proteostasis.
claims.source: Our data suggest that by SUMOylating CAR-1, the IIS suppresses its activity, thereby activating glp-1 to shorten lifespan and impair proteostasis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including SUMOylation data, lifespan assays, and proteostasis assays.

claims.claim: K185 and K257 are located within predicted SUMOylation motifs in CAR-1.
claims.source: To directly address this, we used the computational tool GPS-SUMO (Zhao et al., 2014), for identifying SUMOylation consensus motifs in the sequence of CAR-1. Two lysine residues, K185 and K257 were found to be located within predicted SUMOylation motifs.
claims.evidence: Supported by computational prediction using GPS-SUMO tool.

claims.claim: K185 is more likely to serve as a SUMOylation site than K257.
claims.source: Among the two, K185 is more likely to serve as a SUMOylation site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CAR-1 is SUMOylated on more than one site.
claims.source: Our results also show that CAR-1 is SUMOylated on more than one site, as the substitution of either K185 or of K257 with arginine, did not abolish SUMOylation of the protein.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The lifespan-shortening effect of car-1 RNAi is less prominent than that of daf-16 RNAi.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the car-1 RNAi-mediated lifespan shortening effect was less prominent than that of daf-16 RNAi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, mean LS of 12.19 ± 0.44 days).
claims.evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The lifespan-controlling functions of car-1 are DAF-16 dependent.
claims.source: This observation implies that the lifespan regulatory functions of car-1 are DAF-16 dependent.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that car-1 RNAi has no effect on lifespan in daf-16 mutant worms.

claims.claim: The lifespans of daf-9 and daf-12 mutant worms are shortened by car-1 RNAi.
claims.source: To test this, we followed the lifespans of daf-9 (strain CF2531) and of daf-12 (strain AA86) mutant worms that were either treated with daf-16, car-1 RNAi or left untreated, and found that the lifespans of both worm strains were shortened by daf-16 RNAi as well as by the knockdown of car-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, A and B, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: car-1 RNAi shortens lifespan by a daf-9 and daf-12-independent mechanism.
claims.source: The similar rates of lifespan shortening that resulted from the knockdown of car-1 in wild-type worms (Figure 2A), daf-9 and daf-12 mutant worms, strongly suggest that car-1 RNAi shortens lifespan by a daf-9 and daf-12-independent mechanism.
claims.evidence: Inferred from similar lifespan shortening effects of car-1 RNAi in wild-type, daf-9, and daf-12 mutant worms.

claims.claim: The over-expression of wild-type CAR-1 has no effect on lifespan.
claims.source: The over-expression of wild-type CAR-1 has no effect on lifespan, as animals that express this protein and wild-type worms had very similar lifespans (16.15 ± 0.46 and 15.82 ± 0.39 days respectively, p=0.297).
claims.evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 by RNAi enhances physiological apoptosis in hermaphrodites.
claims.source: The knockdown of car-1 by RNAi was reported to enhance physiological apoptosis in hermaphrodites (Boag et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Boag et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 elevates the number of apoptotic nuclei in the gonad by approximately 2.5 fold.
claims.source: Our results (Figure 3E) indicate that, as shown previously (Boag et al., 2005), the knockdown of car-1 elevates the number of apoptotic nuclei in the gonad by approximately 2.5 fold.
claims.evidence: Supported by apoptosis quantification data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Boag et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 reduces the brood size of wild-type worms by approximately 45%.
claims.source: While untreated N2 worms laid on average 244 eggs in total, their car-1 RNAi-treated counterparts laid only 133 eggs (a reduction of ~ 45% (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D)).
claims.evidence: Supported by egg-laying assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The knockdown of car-1 reduces the brood size of kri-1 mutant worms by approximately 91%.
claims.source: The knockdown of car-1 by RNAi resulted in ~ 46% reduction in the brood size of N2 worms (average numbers of progeny 244 and 133 for untreated and car-1 RNAi treated worms, respectively) and in ~ 91% reduction in CF2052 worms (an average of 116 and 10 living progeny per a single N2 and CF2052 worm, respectively).
claims.evidence: Supported by egg-laying assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: CAR-1 regulates reproduction by GLP-1-dependent and GLP-1-independent mechanisms.
claims.source: Altogether, despite the similarity in the number of germ cells in car-1 RNAi-treated and untreated N2 worms, the reduction in brood size of wild-type worms by car-1 RNAi, strongly suggests that CAR-1 regulates reproduction by GLP-1-dependent and GLP-1-independent mechanisms.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that car-1 RNAi reduces brood size despite not affecting germ cell number, and from effects in various mutant backgrounds.

claims.claim: CAR-1 is a component of the reproduction-regulating mechanism downstream of the IIS.
claims.source: In addition, our observation that the knockdown of car-1 leads to nearly complete sterility of worms carrying weak kri-1 or daf-2 alleles or nonfunctional daf-16, suggests that CAR-1 is also a component of the reproduction-regulating mechanism downstream of the IIS.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the severe sterility phenotype of car-1 RNAi in daf-2, daf-16, and kri-1 mutant backgrounds.

claims.claim: The egg-laying modulation resulting from car-1 knockdown is dependent on functional daf-9 and daf-12.
claims.source: These observations show that the egg-laying modulation that resulted from the knockdown of car-1 by RNAi is dependent on the presence of functional daf-9 and daf-12, linking CAR-1 also with the DAF-9/DAF-12 pathway.
claims.evidence: Supported by the observation that car-1 RNAi does not affect egg-laying in daf-9 and daf-12 mutants.

claims.claim: Abolishing the nematode's ability to resist heat by knocking down neuronal components provides partial protection from proteotoxicity.
claims.source: However, it has been already shown that abolishing the nematode's ability to resist heat by knocking down neuronal components, provides the worm with partial protection from proteotoxicity (Prahlad and Morimoto, 2011; Volovik et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Prahlad and Morimoto, 2011 and Volovik et al., 2014b.

claims.claim: Transcriptional co-factors can differentially affect the expression of different target genes.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with the finding that in some cases, transcriptional co-factors affect the expression of some target genes but not of others (Volovik et al., 2014b), and show the complex regulatory relations between car-1 and glp-1.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Volovik et al., 2014b.

claims.claim: The knockdown of nhl-1 lowers the expression of sod-3 and sip-1 but has no effect on mtl-1 expression.
claims.source: For instance, the knockdown of the DAF-16 transcriptional co-factor nhl-1, lowers the expression level of sod-3 and of sip-1, but has no effect on the expression of mtl-1, which are all known target genes of DAF-16 (Volovik et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Volovik et al., 2014b.

claims.claim: CAR-1 negatively regulates DNA-damage-mediated apoptosis.
claims.source: The observed protection from UV radiation, conferred by car-1 RNAi, is consistent with a previous report that CAR-1 and CGH-1 negatively regulate DNA-damage-mediated apoptosis (Tomazella et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tomazella et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The ability to resist stresses such as heat and oxidation are not necessarily coupled with lifespan determination.
claims.source: These results support the theme that the ability to resist stresses such as heat (Maman et al., 2013; Volovik et al., 2014b) and oxidation (Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2012) are not necessarily coupled with lifespan determination.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Maman et al., 2013; Volovik et al., 2014b; Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2012.

claims.claim: SMK-1 is needed for resistance to UV radiation and pathogenic bacteria but is dispensable for heat stress resistance.
claims.source: For instance, the transcription factor SMK-1 is needed for the worm to resist UV radiation and pathogenic bacteria but is dispensable for coping with heat (Wolff et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wolff et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The knockdown of caveolin-1 extends lifespan and provides partial protection from pathogenic bacteria but has no role in heat stress resistance.
claims.source: Similarly, we recently reported that the knockdown of caveolin-1 extends lifespan and provides partial protection from pathogenic bacteria, but has no role in heat stress resistance (Roitenberg et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Roitenberg et al., 2018.

claims.claim: SUMOylation serves as a functional switch of CAR-1 governed by the IIS.
claims.source: In this study, we unveiled a novel role of SUMOylation in the regulation of aging, serving as a functional switch of CAR-1, which is governed by the IIS.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that IIS reduction lowers CAR-1 SUMOylation and that SUMOylation-resistant CAR-1 K185R extends lifespan.

claims.claim: Reduced IIS may lower AKT activity, resulting in SMO-1 destabilization and reduction of UBC-9 activity.
claims.source: One possible explanation stems from the correlation between AKT function, the stability of SUMO, and the SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBC-9 in mammals (Lin et al., 2016). According to this theme, reduced IIS lowers AKT activity, resulting in SMO-1 destabilization and in reduction of UBC-9 activity.
claims.evidence: Speculative mechanism based on citation to Lin et al., 2016.

claims.claim: IIS reduction may lower the expression of genes encoding proteins involved in CAR-1 SUMOylation.
claims.source: Alternatively, the expression of specific genes that encode for proteins involved in CAR-1 SUMOylation may be positively regulated by the IIS, which lowers the expression of these genes and reduces the rate of CAR-1 SUMOylation.
claims.evidence: Speculative alternative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: IIS reduction protects from proteotoxicity and extends lifespan by additional CAR-1-independent mechanisms.
claims.source: On one hand, these observations suggest that IIS reduction also protects from proteotoxicity and extends lifespan by additional, CAR-1-independent mechanisms.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that simultaneous knockdown of car-1 and daf-2 only partially reduces the protective effects of daf-2 RNAi.

claims.claim: SUMOylation controls the localization of the IGF-1 receptor and its signaling activity in mammalian tissues.
claims.source: Phosphorylation regulates the activities of DAF-16, SKN-1, and HSF-1 downstream of the IIS (Lee et al., 2001; Tullet et al., 2008; Chiang et al., 2012) and SUMOylation controls the localization of the IGF-1 receptor and its signaling activity in mammalian tissues (Sehat et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sehat et al., 2010.

claims.claim: SUMOylation is critical for aging-associated modulation of mevalonate biosynthesis.
claims.source: SUMOylation is also critical for aging-associated modulation of mevalonate biosynthesis (Sapir et al., 2014), a metabolite that has been implicated in the development of clinical conditions (Mokarram et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sapir et al., 2014 and Mokarram et al., 2017.

claims.claim: kri-1 is essential for the mediation of longevity by germ cell ablation but not by IIS reduction.
claims.source: kri-1 is essential for the mediation of longevity by germ cell ablation but not by IIS reduction (Berman and Kenyon, 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Berman and Kenyon, 2006.

claims.claim: The TGF-β pathway converges with the IIS at the nuclear hormone receptor DAF-12.
claims.source: This pathway converges with the IIS at the nuclear hormone receptor DAF-12, whose activation is regulated by the cytochrome P450 enzyme, DAF-9 (Gerisch et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gerisch et al., 2001.

claims.claim: GLP-1 is involved in germ cell proliferation and reproduction.
claims.source: Beside its roles in lifespan determination, GLP-1 is also involved in germ cells proliferation and reproduction (Austin and Kimble, 1987).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Austin and Kimble, 1987.

claims.claim: The expression of Aβ causes progressive paralysis in C. elegans.
claims.source: To address this, we utilized worms that express the Alzheimer's disease associated, human Aβ3-42 peptide (McColl et al., 2009), in their body wall muscles (strain CL2006, Aβ worms) (Link, 1995). The expression of Aβ causes progressive paralysis within the worm population, a phenotype that can be alleviated by the knockdown of daf-2 (Cohen et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to McColl et al., 2009; Link, 1995; Cohen et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Expanded glutamine stretches cause various human neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington's disease.
claims.source: Expanded glutamine stretches cause various human neurodegenerative maladies, including Huntington's disease (Bates, 2003), and lead to impaired neuronal activity in worms (Vilchez et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bates, 2003 and Vilchez et al., 2012.

results.result: IIS reduction modulates global SUMOylation patterns and specifically reduces CAR-1 SUMOylation approximately threefold without affecting CAR-1 protein levels or car-1 gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence from western blots (C1), mass spectrometry (C2, C3), and protein quantification (C5) demonstrating that daf-2 RNAi reduces CAR-1 SUMOylation while maintaining stable CAR-1 protein levels. The multiple independent experimental approaches strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: CAR-1 contains multiple SUMOylation sites, with K185 and K257 identified as predicted SUMOylation motifs, and K185 being the more likely site.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by computational prediction (GPS-SUMO tool) and immunoprecipitation data showing that mutation of either K185 or K257 alone does not abolish SUMOylation, confirming multiple modification sites. The computational and experimental approaches are complementary.

results.result: SUMOylation of CAR-1 at lysine 185, but not lysine 257, regulates lifespan, as CAR-1 K185R expression extends lifespan by approximately 53% while CAR-1 K257R has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C48 demonstrate site-specific effects of SUMOylation on lifespan through multiple independent experiments showing significant lifespan extension with K185R mutation but not K257R mutation. The differential effects of the two mutations provide strong evidence for K185-specific regulation.

results.result: car-1 is required for normal lifespan and full longevity of daf-2 mutants in a DAF-16-dependent manner, as car-1 knockout or RNAi shortens lifespan in wild-type and daf-2 mutant worms but has no effect in daf-16 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C72-C73 provide consistent evidence across multiple genetic backgrounds showing that car-1 regulates lifespan through DAF-16. The lack of effect in daf-16 mutants (C11) combined with lifespan shortening in wild-type and daf-2 mutants (C9-C10) establishes epistatic relationships.

results.result: CAR-1 K185R-mediated longevity requires DAF-16, but CAR-1 also regulates lifespan through DAF-16-independent mechanisms, as daf-16 RNAi reduces CAR-1 K185R worm lifespan to wild-type levels rather than below.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C49 present an apparent paradox: CAR-1 K185R longevity is DAF-16-dependent (C12), yet the authors infer DAF-16-independent mechanisms exist (C49) because daf-16 RNAi doesn't shorten lifespan below wild-type. This interpretation is speculative and could alternatively reflect incomplete RNAi knockdown or ceiling effects in short-lived worms. Additional experiments are needed to definitively establish DAF-16-independent mechanisms.

results.result: CAR-1 mediates its lifespan effects through the GLP-1 pathway, as car-1 RNAi does not affect lifespan in glp-1 or kri-1 mutant worms, suggesting CAR-1 negatively regulates GLP-1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 and C46-C47 demonstrate genetic epistasis through loss-of-function experiments showing car-1 RNAi has no effect when glp-1 or kri-1 are mutated. This places CAR-1 upstream or parallel to GLP-1 in the longevity pathway. The inference of negative regulation (C47) is supported by gene expression data.

results.result: car-1 regulates lifespan independently of the daf-9/daf-12 pathway, as car-1 RNAi shortens lifespan similarly in wild-type, daf-9, and daf-12 mutant worms.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 show that car-1 RNAi produces similar lifespan shortening effects across different genetic backgrounds (wild-type, daf-9, daf-12 mutants), indicating independence from the TGF-β/steroid hormone pathway. The similar magnitude of effects supports pathway independence.

results.result: CAR-1 regulates germ cell number in a dose-dependent manner: car-1 RNAi has no effect, wild-type CAR-1 overexpression reduces germ cells, and CAR-1 K185R overexpression further reduces germ cells by approximately 22%.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 and C15 demonstrate dose-dependent effects through germ cell counting experiments. The graded response (no effect → reduction → greater reduction) with increasing CAR-1 activity supports a direct regulatory role. However, the lack of effect with car-1 RNAi (C50) is explained by the authors as due to SUMOylation-mediated inactivation.

results.result: car-1 RNAi and CAR-1 K185R expression both increase germline apoptosis approximately 2.5-fold and 80% respectively, despite having opposite effects on lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 and C77-C78 are supported by acridine orange staining data showing increased apoptosis with both car-1 knockdown and K185R overexpression. However, this creates an apparent paradox where both interventions increase apoptosis but have opposite lifespan effects, suggesting apoptosis level alone doesn't determine longevity outcomes.

results.result: CAR-1 K185R expression reduces brood size to approximately 105 progeny compared to 271 in wild-type worms, while car-1 RNAi reduces brood size by 45% in wild-type and 91% in kri-1 mutant worms.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C79-C80 are supported by egg-laying assays showing consistent reductions in progeny across different genetic manipulations. The more severe effect in kri-1 mutants (C80) suggests genetic interaction between car-1 and kri-1 in reproduction control.

results.result: CAR-1 regulates reproduction through both GLP-1-dependent and GLP-1-independent mechanisms, with effects dependent on functional daf-9 and daf-12, as car-1 RNAi causes near-sterility in daf-2 and daf-16 mutants but has no effect in daf-9 and daf-12 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 and C81-C83 demonstrate complex genetic interactions through egg-laying assays in multiple mutant backgrounds. The differential effects across genetic backgrounds support multiple regulatory mechanisms. However, the severe sterility in daf-2/daf-16 mutants could reflect additive defects rather than specific pathway interactions.

results.result: GLP-1 positively regulates car-1 expression (approximately 65% reduction when glp-1 is inactivated) and the expression of its target genes sygl-1 and lst-1, establishing a regulatory circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C54 are supported by qPCR data showing temperature-dependent effects in glp-1 mutants. The reciprocal regulation between CAR-1 and GLP-1 suggests a feedback loop. However, the magnitude of car-1 reduction (65%) is substantial and could have pleiotropic effects.

results.result: CAR-1 differentially regulates GLP-1 target genes, negatively controlling sygl-1 expression (increased upon car-1 knockdown) but positively affecting lst-1 expression (decreased upon car-1 knockdown).
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C55-C56 demonstrate gene-specific regulatory effects through qPCR in daf-2 mutants. The opposing effects on different GLP-1 targets indicate CAR-1 acts as a context-dependent co-regulator rather than a simple repressor. This complexity is consistent with transcriptional co-factor biology.

results.result: CAR-1 regulates Aβ proteotoxicity in a DAF-16-dependent manner: car-1 RNAi increases paralysis, concurrent daf-2/car-1 knockdown partially protects, and CAR-1 K185R expression provides significant protection from day 7 onward.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 provide consistent evidence from paralysis assays across five independent experiments showing CAR-1's role in proteostasis. The partial protection with concurrent knockdown (C24) and DAF-16 dependence (C26) establish mechanistic relationships. The delayed protection onset (day 7, C25) suggests age-dependent effects.

results.result: CAR-1 controls polyglutamine proteotoxicity through GLP-1, as car-1 RNAi decreases motility in polyQ67-YFP worms at day 4 and enhances paralysis in polyQ35-YFP worms but not in polyQ35-YFP/glp-1 double mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 and C57 demonstrate GLP-1-dependent proteostasis regulation through genetic epistasis experiments. The lack of car-1 RNAi effect in glp-1 mutants (C28) provides strong evidence for pathway dependence. The age-specific effect at day 4 (C27) indicates progressive proteotoxicity.

results.result: The CAR-1-associated RNA helicase CGH-1 also modulates lifespan and proteostasis, as cgh-1 RNAi significantly increases paralysis rates in Aβ worms, suggesting CAR-1 and CGH-1 cooperatively regulate proteostasis through GLP-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C58-C60 extend the CAR-1 findings to its binding partner CGH-1 through parallel experiments. The similar effects of car-1 and cgh-1 RNAi on proteotoxicity support a cooperative mechanism. However, the inference that both act through GLP-1 (C60) is based primarily on analogy to CAR-1 rather than direct testing of CGH-1/GLP-1 epistasis.

results.result: car-1 has minimal effects on heat stress resistance: car-1 RNAi shows no significant effect in CF512 and N2 worms, while CAR-1 K185R expression provides modest but significant protection (p<0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are supported by heat stress survival assays, though the effects are small. The lack of car-1 RNAi effect (C30) contrasts with the modest K185R protection (C31), suggesting SUMOylation state matters for heat resistance. However, the small effect size and marginal significance (p<0.04) warrant cautious interpretation.

results.result: CAR-1 has opposing effects on different stress responses: car-1 RNAi provides small but significant protection against P. aeruginosa and UV radiation, while CAR-1 overexpression (wild-type or K185R) reduces survival after these stresses.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 demonstrate stress-specific and direction-dependent effects through survival assays. The protective effect of car-1 RNAi contrasts with its detrimental effects on proteostasis and lifespan, supporting the authors' conclusion that stress resistance and longevity are uncoupled. The reciprocal effects of knockdown versus overexpression strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: The IIS suppresses CAR-1 activity through SUMOylation at K185, which activates GLP-1 to shorten lifespan and impair proteostasis, with SUMOylation serving as a functional switch governed by IIS.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C91 synthesize multiple experimental observations into a mechanistic model. The model is supported by: (1) IIS reduction lowers CAR-1 SUMOylation, (2) SUMOylation-resistant CAR-1 K185R extends lifespan and protects from proteotoxicity, (3) car-1 acts through GLP-1, and (4) effects are largely DAF-16-dependent. The convergence of genetic, biochemical, and phenotypic data supports this integrative conclusion.

results.result: Two potential mechanisms are proposed for how IIS controls CAR-1 SUMOylation: (1) IIS reduction lowers AKT activity, destabilizing SMO-1 and reducing UBC-9 activity, or (2) IIS positively regulates expression of genes encoding CAR-1 SUMOylation machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 present speculative mechanisms without direct experimental support. C92 is based on mammalian studies (Lin et al., 2016) that may not apply to C. elegans, and C93 is purely hypothetical. Neither mechanism is tested in this study. The differential SUMOylation of different proteins upon IIS reduction (Figure 1A) argues against a global SMO-1 destabilization mechanism (C92).

results.result: IIS reduction protects from proteotoxicity and extends lifespan through additional CAR-1-independent mechanisms, as simultaneous daf-2 and car-1 knockdown only partially reduces daf-2 RNAi protective effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is supported by the observation that concurrent daf-2/car-1 RNAi still provides partial protection from Aβ paralysis (C24), indicating CAR-1 is not the sole mediator of IIS effects. However, the interpretation is complicated by potential additive effects and incomplete RNAi knockdown. Additional experiments with complete loss-of-function alleles would strengthen this conclusion.
